blocks.label: The short of it

blocks.html:
The short answer

We agree with most of this, and we'd like to do all of it. The stage-based flows are the biggest opportunity in the account, the quiz flow deserves far more traffic, the subscription flow isn't reaching the people it should, and the SMS programme should come off until it's rebuilt. We'll take that on inside the current retainer.

The one place we'd push back is cutting campaign volume. Not because the instinct is wrong, the list is expensive and worth protecting, but because the account has already run the experiment and it points the other way. Here's the evidence, then what we'd do instead.

Where the unsubscribes come from

Over the last 12 months, 67,130 unsubscribes came from campaigns and 11,563 from flows. So campaigns are the bulk of it, which supports the worry.

Per email delivered, though, it reverses. Flows unsubscribe at 0.60% against 0.23% for campaigns, 2.6 times worse. Campaigns only dominate the total because they send more. The heaviest single losses in the account are flow messages: ZM // Welcome Flow at 0.78%, ZM // Welcome Flow (SMS) PHASING OUT at 4.44%, ZM // Abandoned Browse at 0.77%. That gives the flow rebuild a second payoff nobody has counted yet: those flows are leaking list as well as under-earning.

blocks.cap: 52 weeks, Sep ’25 to Aug ’26. Bars are what the week earned, the line is the unsubscribe rate per recipient at that cadence.
blocks.title: What each cadence earns, and what it costs in unsubscribes

blocks.html:
It isn't the cadence

Sends per week against the unsubscribe rate is -0.54. The more campaigns in a week, the lower the rate per recipient. The five worst weeks of the year for unsubscribes were all one and two send weeks; the six and seven send weeks are the cleanest in the account. Cadence drives the unsubscribe count (+0.64) only because it drives volume.

And the last two quarters are the experiment itself. From Mar ’26 you sent 44 campaigns and earned $138,568 at $0.0177 per recipient and a 0.191% unsubscribe rate. In the quarter to Aug ’26 you sent 60, up 36%, and earned $175,389, up 27%, at $0.0232 per recipient and 0.183%. More sending went with better revenue per recipient and a lower unsubscribe rate, in the same window this review covers.

Taking the account's own growth out of it, sends against weekly revenue is +0.72 and sends against revenue per campaign is -0.17, which is no measurable decline in what an individual campaign earns as volume rises.

blocks.cap: 70 email campaigns over the last 120 days, each a bar. The line is the median at 0.183%.
blocks.title: Every campaign's unsubscribe rate, worst to best

blocks.html:
And it isn't one or two bad emails

Across 70 campaigns the unsubscribe rate runs from 0.108% to 0.294%, with a median of 0.183%. The worst single campaign accounts for 2.5% of the period's unsubscribes. There's no offender to remove and nothing broken to fix. This is simply what a send to a warm list costs.

Who the campaigns already go to

This part matters, because recipient counts can look like a blanket send when they aren't. Campaigns go to ZM // 90D Engaged + Apple Privacy False (201,503 profiles), 10 of the last 15 sends, and every one of them also excludes DA | 4+ Soft Bounces, ZM // List Hygiene - Bad Emails, ZM // List Hygiene - Dead (180 Days), ZM // List Hygiene - Engagement Exclusion: 10 Emails and more. Against a file of 677,226 profiles, that's already a tightly filtered audience rather than the whole list, and the hygiene segments doing the filtering are ours.

Which is why we don't think there's a suppression win left to take. The 0.23% we pay is being paid on people who engaged in the last 90 days, and that is a normal cost rather than a symptom.

There is room in the other direction. Campaigns go to the 90-day engaged group, while the 180-day engaged group is 254,039 people. That's about 52,536 people who engaged in the last three to six months and currently receive no campaigns at all, which is where the next section goes.

What we'd do instead, and it's more work not less

1. Rebuild the stage-based flows, prioritised by cohort size. Agreed, and it's first. They're the weakest per-recipient performers in the account and the highest-intent audience in it, and they're also among the worst for unsubscribes, so the rebuild pays twice.

2. Campaign cadence: hold it, and improve the targeting. The stage-targeted sends already earn $0.0274 per recipient against $0.0226 for the blanket sends to the engaged segment, +21%. So the lever is which people get which campaign, not how many campaigns go out. Your own stage-targeting works, which is also the best argument that the stage-based flows will.

3. An evergreen best-of flow, sending proven campaigns to people we don't currently reach. The ten best campaigns of the last 120 days averaged $0.0305 per recipient against a $0.0221 median, at a 0.201% unsubscribe rate, below the account average. Right now that content goes out once and stops. On a flow it keeps earning, and it gives us something worth sending to those 52,536 warm people outside the campaign audience. It will pull the average revenue per recipient across the flows down, and that's fine: it's a campaign on a flow rail, so judging it by flow averages measures the wrong thing. What it adds is incremental.

4. Quiz reach, subscription flow coverage, and SMS. Agreed on all three. The quiz is the best-performing thing in the account and reaching almost nobody, the subscription flow reaching 4,728 people against roughly 12,000 orders a month reads as a trigger fault rather than a performance one, and the SMS programme should come off until it earns its place. Switching it off is the one instance where sending less is unambiguously right.

What this costs. Nothing. We're taking the flow rebuild, the evergreen build and the campaign work at the current rate. We've been getting more efficient and we'd rather put that into the account than into our margin. Let's look at scope again in six months once the flows are rebuilt and we can see what they're doing.

52 weeks of your own campaign sends, Sep ’25 to Aug ’26, grouped by campaigns per week, plus every email campaign of the last 120 days at individual level. Unsubscribes are split by source using each channel's own delivered volume, so the rates are per email sent rather than per person on the list.

Correlations are Pearson. The revenue ones are detrended, which removes the straight-line growth in the account from both sides before comparing them, so "busier weeks earned more" cannot be mistaken for "sending more changed what a send earns". Revenue is Klaviyo attributed on last click, so it's the generous reading rather than the truth; a holdout is the only way to get the strict one and we're happy to run one.
